why_how.text: Driving demands full attention and quick reactions, so your health and alertness are part of being fit to drive.
A tired driver can drift or doze for a moment, and at highway speed that moment covers a long distance.

scenario.text: Kai is driving alone on a fast rural highway late at night and keeps yawning and drifting toward the rumble strip.

reasoning.text: Yawning again and again and drifting out of the lane are signs of drowsiness, and drowsy crashes happen most on fast rural roads with a lone driver.

result.text: Kai stops at the next safe place, takes a short nap, and plans regular breaks for the rest of the trip.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a nap and a cup of coffee fix fatigue for the rest of a long trip.

correction.text: A short nap with caffeine is only a temporary help; the long-trip habit is a stop at least every two hours.

prompt.text: Kai keeps yawning and drifting toward the rumble strip on a quiet rural highway. What should Kai do?

answer.text: Stop driving at a safe place; a nap and caffeine help only for a while.

rationale.text: Those are drowsiness signs, and the handbook says a tired driver should stop rather than push on.

narration.text: This chapter turns from the rules of the road to the condition of the driver and the protection of everyone in the vehicle. It starts with your health and alertness. Both physical and mental health shape how you drive, and a driver license requires that you be in good health. In this lesson you will learn how even a short illness can slow you down, why a brief nod-off at highway speed is so dangerous, where drowsy crashes tend to happen, the warning signs of drowsiness, and what to do about fatigue before and during a long drive.

lines.text: A cold or flu can slow you.

narration.text: Both physical and mental health shape how you drive, and the license itself assumes you are in good health. That does not only mean serious conditions. Even a short illness such as a cold, a headache or the flu can leave you less alert and slower to respond behind the wheel. Cold medicine, a pounding headache or a fever all pull attention away from the road. So on a day when you feel sick, it is worth asking whether the trip is necessary, whether someone else can drive, and whether you can wait until you are feeling better before getting behind the wheel.

lines.text: Fifty-five miles per hour covers a field fast.
Drowsy crashes tend to be serious.

narration.text: At fifty-five miles per hour, a vehicle covers the length of a football field in three point seven seconds. So even a brief nod-off, the kind that feels like a long blink, can carry you across a lane or off the road. Crashes caused by drowsiness tend to be serious, and they happen most often on fast rural highways when the driver is traveling alone. The pattern makes sense: long, quiet stretches with no one to talk to make it easy for sleepiness to creep in, and high speed means there is little time to recover once your eyes close.

Learn to recognize drowsiness before it becomes sleep. The signs include not remembering the last few miles you drove, hitting a rumble strip or drifting out of your lane, yawning again and again, and struggling to focus or keep your eyes open. Any one of these is a warning that your brain is starting to shut down, even if you do not feel asleep. Many drivers try to fight through it by turning up the radio or opening a window. Those tricks do not restore alertness. The signs mean it is time to change the plan, not to push harder.

If you grow tired while driving, you should stop. A nap of fifteen to forty-five minutes and some caffeine help only for a while, so treat them as a short bridge, not a cure. Prevention works better. On a long drive, take a break at least every two hours: leave the car, stretch and walk briskly. The handbook also suggests capping your driving at about three hundred to four hundred miles a day, and avoiding medicines that make you drowsy. Planning these limits before the trip makes it easier to stick to them when you are tempted to keep going.

Here is the trap. Many drivers believe that a short nap and a strong coffee solve fatigue for the rest of the trip. They do not. A short nap with caffeine is only a temporary help for fatigue, while the long-trip habit is a stop at least every two hours. So if a practice question asks what a tired driver should do, the best answer is to stop, and if it asks how to manage a long drive, the answer is regular breaks. An option that treats caffeine as a replacement for rest, or suggests pushing on with the window down, is the wrong one.

Here is a quick check: Kai is driving alone late at night on a fast rural highway. Kai keeps yawning, cannot remember the last few miles, and has just hit the rumble strip at the edge of the lane. What should Kai do? Work it out before reading on. The answer is to stop driving at the next safe place. These are clear signs of drowsiness, on exactly the kind of road where drowsy crashes happen most. A nap of fifteen to forty-five minutes and some caffeine may help for a while, and after that Kai should plan breaks at least every two hours.

lines.text: Stop, nap briefly, break every two hours.

narration.text: Let us recap. A license requires good health, and even a cold, a headache or the flu can make you less alert and slower to respond. At fifty-five miles per hour a car covers a football field in three point seven seconds, so a brief nod-off is dangerous, and drowsy crashes are most common on fast rural highways with a lone driver. Watch for lost miles, rumble strips, lane drifting, repeated yawning and heavy eyes. If tired, stop; naps and caffeine help only briefly. Break at least every two hours and cap the day at about three hundred to four hundred miles.

why_how.text: Driving is a full-time job, so anything that takes your eyes, hands or mind off it raises crash risk.
Many distractions take a hand off the wheel, which leaves less control in an emergency.

scenario.text: Avery's phone buzzes with a call while Avery is driving with a friend in the passenger seat.

reasoning.text: The handbook advises letting a passenger make calls and letting unanswered calls go to a message.

result.text: Avery lets the call go to a message and keeps both hands on the wheel.

claim.text: Many people think distraction only means texting.

correction.text: Distracted driving is any activity that might pull attention from the main job of driving, including eating, grooming, maps, navigation and audio controls.

prompt.text: Avery's phone rings while driving and a friend is in the passenger seat. What does the handbook recommend?

answer.text: Let the friend take the call, or let it go to a message.

rationale.text: Phone use while driving should happen only when truly necessary, and a passenger can handle the call.

narration.text: This lesson is about distraction, one of the most common causes of crashes and one of the easiest to prevent. You will learn what the handbook means by distracted driving, the everyday activities that count as distractions, what distraction does to your reactions and awareness, why it makes crashes harder to avoid, and the phone habits the handbook recommends. The next lesson covers the phone laws themselves. Here the focus is on the habits that keep your eyes on the road, your hands on the wheel and your mind on the job of driving.

lines.text: Any activity that pulls attention away.

narration.text: Distracted driving means any activity that might pull your attention away from the main job of driving. That definition is broad on purpose. Common distractions include texting, phone use, eating or drinking, talking with passengers, grooming, reading maps, using navigation, watching video and adjusting audio equipment. Some of these feel harmless because people do them every day. But each one shifts some attention away from the road, and attention is limited. The more of it a task takes, the less is left for spotting a hazard, judging a gap, or reacting to a sudden change ahead.

lines.text: Often a hand off the wheel.

narration.text: Distracted drivers respond more slowly to events such as a car slowing to turn or pulling out of a side road, and they miss hazards like pedestrians or debris more often. Many distractions also make it harder to steer clear of a crash because they take at least one hand off the steering wheel. So distraction attacks safety in two ways at once. It delays the moment you notice danger, and it weakens your ability to respond once you do. The result is that a situation a focused driver handles easily can become a crash for a distracted one.

lines.text: Food, grooming, maps and music count.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many learners think distracted driving simply means texting, so they relax about everything else. The handbook's definition is much wider. Distracted driving means any activity that might pull your attention away from the main job of driving. Eating, drinking, grooming, reading maps, setting the navigation, watching video and adjusting audio equipment all count, and so does an absorbing conversation with a passenger. On practice questions, an option that limits distraction to phones alone is wrong. If a task pulls your eyes, hands or mind away from driving, it is a distraction.

lines.text: Use the phone only when truly necessary.
Let a passenger make the call.
Let calls go to a message.

narration.text: The handbook gives practical phone habits. Use a phone while driving only when truly necessary, for emergencies or to reach a parent, legal guardian or spouse, and only at a safe time and place. Let a passenger make the call for you, let unanswered calls go to a message, and secure the phone so it cannot fly around in a crash. A loose phone can become a dangerous object in a sudden stop. These habits work together: fewer calls, handled by someone else when possible, with the phone stowed where it will not distract you or turn into a projectile.

lines.text: A call comes in while driving.
A friend sits in the passenger seat.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Avery is driving across town with a friend in the passenger seat when Avery's phone starts ringing. It is not an emergency. What does the handbook recommend? Work it out before reading on. The answer is to let the friend take the call, or simply let it go to a message. The handbook advises using a phone while driving only when truly necessary, letting a passenger make calls, and letting unanswered calls go to voicemail. Avery keeps both hands on the wheel and attention on the road, and returns the call after parking.

lines.text: Let it ring; let a passenger help.

narration.text: To wrap up, distracted driving means any activity that might pull your attention from the main job of driving, from texting and phone calls to eating, grooming, maps, navigation, video and audio controls. Distracted drivers respond more slowly and miss hazards more often, and many distractions take a hand off the wheel. Use a phone only when truly necessary and only at a safe time and place, let a passenger make calls, let unanswered calls go to a message, and secure the phone so it cannot fly around in a crash. Next, the phone laws that back these habits up.

why_how.text: Texting and email take eyes, hands and mind off the road at once, so North Carolina bans them for every driver.
Young drivers and school bus drivers carry extra risk or responsibility, so the law bans phone use for them entirely.

scenario.text: Jordan, age seventeen, is driving home and wants to make a quick hands-free call to a friend.

reasoning.text: A driver under eighteen may not use a cell phone or related technology at all while the vehicle is moving, except to call nine one one in an emergency.

result.text: Jordan waits until the car is parked before calling the friend.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the texting ban is the only phone law for drivers under eighteen.

correction.text: Every driver is barred from texting or email, but a driver under eighteen may not use a phone at all while moving, except for an emergency call to nine one one.

prompt.text: Jordan is seventeen and wants to make a hands-free call to a friend while driving. Is that allowed?

answer.text: No. Under eighteen, no phone use at all while the car is moving, except an emergency call to nine one one.

rationale.text: The under-eighteen ban covers all phone technology, hands-free included, unlike the all-driver texting ban.

narration.text: The last lesson covered habits. This one covers the law. North Carolina has a phone rule for every driver, a stricter rule for drivers under eighteen, and a special rule for school bus drivers. You will learn each of them, and you will also learn to separate the laws from the safety advice that surrounds them. That distinction matters on practice questions, which sometimes present good advice as if it were a legal requirement, or present a legal ban as if it were optional. By the end, you should be able to say which rule applies to which driver.

lines.text: Public streets, highways and vehicular areas.

narration.text: North Carolina makes it unlawful to text or email on a cell phone while driving on a public street, highway or public vehicular area. This applies to every driver, regardless of age or license type. Public vehicular areas include places like parking lots open to the public, so the ban does not switch off when you leave the main road. Texting and email are singled out because they combine all three kinds of distraction at once: your eyes leave the road, your hand leaves the wheel, and your mind leaves the job of driving to compose or read a message.

lines.text: Under eighteen: no phone while moving.
Exception: an emergency call to nine one one.

narration.text: Drivers under eighteen face a stricter rule. A driver under eighteen may not use a cell phone or related technology at all while the vehicle is moving, except to call nine one one in an emergency. That includes hands-free calls and connected technology, not only texting. School bus drivers face a ban too. No one may drive a school bus on a public road or vehicular area while using a cell phone or other mobile-device technology. In both cases the law removes phone use entirely, because young drivers are still learning and school bus drivers carry children.

lines.text: Every driver: no texting or email.
Under eighteen: no phone at all.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Every driver is barred from texting or emailing while driving, but a driver under eighteen is barred from using a phone at all while moving, apart from an emergency call to nine one one. Practice questions often describe a seventeen-year-old making a hands-free call and offer answers that treat it as legal because it is not texting. It is not legal for that driver. On the other side, an adult making a hands-free call is not breaking the texting ban. Check the driver's age first, then decide which rule applies. The memory line: all no texts, teens none.

lines.text: Advice: phone only when truly necessary.

narration.text: Here is a second trap. The texting ban and the under-eighteen ban are laws. Advice to use a phone only for emergencies or to reach family is a safety reminder rather than a separate legal rule. Practice questions may ask which statement is a legal requirement and offer the advice as an option, or ask which is only advice and offer a law. Keep the categories apart. Laws come with penalties and apply to specific drivers. Advice describes the safest habit for everyone. Both matter, but only the laws can bring a ticket or a conviction when they are broken.

Here is a quick check: Jordan is seventeen and driving home from practice. Jordan wants to make a quick hands-free call to a friend through the car's system, with no texting involved. Is that allowed while the car is moving? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no. A driver under eighteen may not use a cell phone or related technology at all while the vehicle is moving, except to call nine one one in an emergency. Hands-free does not change that. Jordan should wait until the car is safely parked before making the call.

lines.text: Every driver: no texting or email.
Under eighteen: no phone, except nine one one.

narration.text: Let us recap the phone laws. North Carolina makes it unlawful for every driver to text or email while driving on a public street, highway or public vehicular area. A driver under eighteen may not use a cell phone or related technology at all while the vehicle is moving, except to call nine one one in an emergency. No one may drive a school bus while using a cell phone or mobile-device technology. And advice to use a phone only when truly necessary is a safety reminder, separate from these legal rules. Next, medicine and alcohol.

why_how.text: Medicines and alcohol both change how the brain works, so they change how you drive.
Alcohol is involved in a large share of traffic deaths, and only time can remove it from a drinker's body.

scenario.text: After a party, Lee has had several drinks and plans to drink coffee and take a cold shower before driving home.

reasoning.text: Only time sobers a drinker; coffee, a large meal or a cold shower will not.

result.text: Lee stays overnight with a friend instead of driving.

claim.text: Many people think coffee or a cold shower can sober up a drinker quickly.

correction.text: Coffee, a big meal and a cold shower do nothing to sober a drinker; only the passing of time does.

prompt.text: Lee has had several drinks and plans to drink strong coffee before driving home. Will that make Lee safe to drive?

answer.text: No. Only time sobers a drinker.

rationale.text: Coffee, food and cold showers do not remove alcohol, so Lee should find another way home.

title.text: What you put in your body

narration.text: This lesson looks at medicine and alcohol from the driver's point of view. The legal side of alcohol was covered in the alcohol and the law chapter. Here the focus is on what these substances do to your ability to drive. You will learn how prescription and over-the-counter medicines can affect driving, how often alcohol is involved in traffic deaths, how alcohol slows the brain and warps judgment, why it makes juggling several tasks so hard, the myth about sobering up quickly, and practical ways to avoid drinking and driving altogether.

lines.text: Learn how a medicine affects you.

narration.text: Both prescription and over-the-counter medicines can affect driving. Allergy pills, cold remedies, pain relievers and many others can cause drowsiness, slower reactions or blurred vision. So the handbook advises learning how a medicine affects you and driving as little as possible while taking it. A good habit is to read the label, ask a pharmacist about side effects, and try a new medicine at home before relying on it for a drive. The long-trip advice from the fatigue lesson fits here too: avoid medicines that make you drowsy when you have a long drive ahead.

lines.text: Involved in about thirty-eight percent of deaths.
A depressant that slows the brain.
Weakens judgment of speed and distance.

narration.text: The handbook states that about thirty-eight percent of all traffic deaths involve alcohol. The reason is clear once you see what alcohol does. Alcohol is a depressant that slows the brain, so you cannot respond, decide or react quickly. It weakens your judgment of speed and of distance to other cars, people or objects, and it gives false confidence that leads to bigger risks. So a drinking driver is slower to see danger, worse at judging it, and more willing to take chances, all at the same time. That combination explains why alcohol shows up in so many fatal crashes.

Driving is a constant juggling act: steering, watching signals, checking mirrors, spotting pedestrians. Alcohol makes it hard to handle more than one task at a time. So while steering, a drinking driver may miss traffic lights, cars coming from side streets, or pedestrians crossing ahead. Alcohol also upsets balance and causes sleepiness, adding the dangers of fatigue on top of impairment. This is why someone who seems to drive straight can still be dangerous. Keeping the car in the lane is only one task, and alcohol steals the attention needed for all the others.

lines.text: Food and cold showers do not work.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Popular myths say a drinker can sober up quickly with strong coffee, a big meal or a cold shower. None of these work. Coffee, a big meal and a cold shower do nothing to sober a drinker; only the passing of time does. Coffee may make a person feel more awake, but the alcohol is still in the blood, still slowing the brain and still weakening judgment. On practice questions, any option offering a quick fix is wrong. The only correct answer to how a drinker sobers up is time. The memory line is three words: only time sobers.

lines.text: Share a taxi or take transit.
Stay over, or ride with a sober driver.

narration.text: Since nothing speeds up sobering, the answer is to plan ahead. Ways to avoid drinking and driving include planning a ride in advance, sharing a taxi, taking public transit, staying overnight with a friend, or riding with someone who has not been drinking. The key word is advance. Decisions made before the first drink are far better than decisions made after several, when judgment is already weakened and false confidence has set in. Agree on a sober driver before the evening starts, or save a ride option on your phone, and the choice is already made.

Here is a quick check: Lee has had several drinks at a party and feels a bit unsteady. Lee plans to drink two cups of strong coffee and then drive home. Will the coffee make Lee safe to drive? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no. Only time sobers a drinker, and coffee, a large meal or a cold shower will not. The coffee might make Lee feel more awake, but the alcohol is still slowing Lee's brain and judgment. Lee should stay overnight, take a taxi or transit, or ride with someone who has not been drinking.

To finish, both prescription and over-the-counter medicines can affect driving, so learn their effects and drive as little as possible while taking them. About thirty-eight percent of traffic deaths involve alcohol. Alcohol is a depressant that slows the brain, weakens judgment of speed and distance, gives false confidence, makes multitasking hard, upsets balance and causes sleepiness. Only time sobers a drinker; coffee, food and cold showers do not. Avoid drinking and driving by planning a ride, sharing a taxi, taking transit, staying over or riding with a sober driver.

why_how.text: Over a lifetime of driving, a serious crash is a real possibility, and seat belts are the main protection when it happens.
Air bags are designed to work with belts, so the law still requires belts, including the lap belt with an automatic harness.

scenario.text: Pat drives a car with automatic shoulder harnesses and air bags, and wonders whether the lap belt matters.

reasoning.text: Seat belts are still required with air bags, and if the vehicle has automatic shoulder harnesses the lap belt must also be worn.

result.text: Pat fastens the lap belt on every trip.

claim.text: Many people think air bags make seat belts optional.

correction.text: Air bags never excuse the seat belt, and a vehicle with an automatic shoulder harness still requires the lap belt.

prompt.text: Pat's car has air bags and automatic shoulder harnesses. Does Pat still need to fasten the lap belt?

answer.text: Yes. The lap belt must be worn with an automatic shoulder harness.

rationale.text: Air bags and harnesses never remove the duty to wear the lap belt.

lines.text: A serious crash is a real risk.

narration.text: This lesson covers seat belts, the single most important safety device in a vehicle. Across a typical lifetime behind the wheel, the odds of a serious injury or death in a crash are roughly one in three, so this is not a remote concern. You will learn who must wear a belt under North Carolina law, why air bags do not replace belts, and the specific exemptions the law allows, from medical conditions and delivery work to farm vehicles and motor homes. The exemptions are narrow, and practice questions test their exact limits, especially the delivery speed rule.

In a vehicle built with seat belts, the driver and every passenger must wear a properly fastened belt whenever the vehicle moves forward on a North Carolina street or highway. Every passenger means every seat, front and back. Properly fastened means worn correctly, not tucked behind the back or under the arm. The odds of a serious crash over a driving lifetime are roughly one in three, and the belt is what keeps you in your seat, away from the windshield and the other occupants, when that crash happens. So the habit is simple: everyone buckles, every trip.

lines.text: Belts required even with air bags.
Automatic harness? Fasten the lap belt too.

narration.text: Seat belts are still required in vehicles with air bags. An air bag is designed to work together with a belt, cushioning a body that the belt is already holding in place. Without the belt, a person can be thrown into the air bag at the wrong angle or slide under it. And if the vehicle has automatic shoulder harnesses, the lap belt must also be worn. The shoulder harness alone leaves the hips free to slide forward in a crash. So in any car, the full belt system is required, and air bags or harnesses are only part of the protection.

lines.text: Lap belt still needed with a harness.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Some people believe that a car with air bags makes seat belts optional, or that an automatic shoulder harness is enough on its own. Both beliefs are wrong. Air bags never excuse the seat belt, and a vehicle with an automatic shoulder harness still requires the lap belt to be fastened. On practice questions, any option suggesting the air bag or the harness replaces the lap belt should be ruled out. Think of the system as layers: the lap belt and shoulder belt hold you, and the air bag adds cushioning on top. The memory line: air bags plus belts.

The seat belt law has narrow exemptions. It exempts an occupant of a noncommercial vehicle whose medical or physical condition, or professionally certified phobia, prevents proper restraint. Rural letter carriers of the Postal Service on duty, and newspaper carriers delivering along their route, are also exempt. Notice how specific these are. Finding a belt uncomfortable is not an exemption, and neither is a short trip. The medical exemption needs a condition or a professionally certified phobia, and the carrier exemptions apply only while the person is on duty along the route.

lines.text: Frequent stops at twenty or slower.
Farm property vehicles within the state.
No belts required, or every seat taken.

narration.text: Drivers or passengers who keep stopping to leave the vehicle or deliver items are exempt, but only if the vehicle goes no faster than twenty miles per hour between stops. Other exemptions cover property-carrying vehicles used for farming within the state, vehicles not legally required to have belts, and situations where every belted or restraint-equipped seat is already taken. In a motor home, occupants other than the driver and front-seat passengers are exempt when the motor home has at least four of the listed living facilities. The front seats of a motor home are never exempt.

Here is a quick check: Pat drives a car with front air bags and automatic shoulder harnesses that slide into place when the door closes. Pat thinks the lap belt is unnecessary with all that equipment. Does Pat still need to fasten the lap belt? Work it out before reading on. The answer is yes. Seat belts are still required in vehicles with air bags, and if the vehicle has automatic shoulder harnesses, the lap belt must also be worn. Air bags and harnesses never remove the duty to wear the lap belt. Pat should buckle it on every trip.

lines.text: Delivery exemption only at twenty or slower.

narration.text: To finish, the lifetime odds of a serious crash injury or death are roughly one in three. In a vehicle built with belts, the driver and every passenger must wear a properly fastened belt whenever it moves forward on a North Carolina road. Belts are required with air bags, and the lap belt is required with automatic shoulder harnesses. Exemptions cover certain medical conditions or certified phobias, on-duty mail and newspaper carriers, frequent-stop deliveries at twenty miles per hour or less, farm property vehicles, vehicles without required belts, full seats, and rear motor home occupants.

why_how.text: Children are smaller and more fragile than adults, so correctly used safety seats prevent most unrestrained child deaths.
The law sets age and weight lines so each child uses the restraint that fits their size.

scenario.text: A parent drives a four-year-old who weighs thirty-five pounds in a car with an active front passenger air bag and a rear seat.

reasoning.text: A child under five weighing under forty pounds must ride in the rear unless the restraint is built for use with a front air bag.

result.text: The parent installs the child's weight-appropriate seat in the rear seat.

claim.text: Common mistake: mixing up the under-eight, under-eighty-pound rule with the under-five, under-forty-pound rule.

correction.text: Under eight and under eighty pounds needs a weight-appropriate restraint; under five and under forty pounds must ride in back near an active front air bag.

prompt.text: A thirty-five-pound four-year-old rides in a car with an active front passenger air bag and a rear seat. Where must the child sit?

answer.text: In the rear seat, unless the restraint is built for use with a front air bag.

rationale.text: The rear-seat rule covers children under five and under forty pounds near an active front air bag.

lines.text: Age and weight decide the restraint.

narration.text: Children depend on adults to keep them safe in a vehicle. Correctly used safety seats could save seven of every ten children who die while riding unrestrained. This lesson covers the rules that make that possible. You will learn how to choose a child seat, the duty a driver has for every passenger under sixteen, the restraint rule for young children based on age and weight, the rear-seat rule when a car has an active front air bag, the narrow lap-belt exception, and how to tell when a child is ready to move from a booster to the adult belt.

A driver carrying any passenger under sixteen must make sure each one is secured in a child restraint or seat belt meeting the federal standards in force when it was made. The duty belongs to the driver, not the passenger or the parent riding along. Within that group, younger children have a stricter rule. A child younger than eight who weighs under eighty pounds must ride in a weight-appropriate child passenger restraint, such as a car seat or booster suited to the child's weight. So the age and the weight together decide whether an adult belt is enough.

title.text: Air bags and the rear seat

lines.text: Active front air bag and a rear seat.
Under five and under forty pounds.
Ride in back unless the restraint allows.

narration.text: Front air bags deploy with enough force to injure a small child. So when a vehicle has an active front passenger air bag and a rear seat, a child under five weighing under forty pounds must ride in the rear, unless the restraint is built for use with a front air bag. Note the conditions. The rule applies when there is an active front passenger air bag and a rear seat to use. If both are true, a young, light child goes in the back. This rule works alongside the under-eight rule; it decides where the child sits, while the other decides what restraint the child uses.

lines.text: Under eight, under eighty: weight-appropriate restraint.
Under five, under forty: rear seat.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Two child rules use age and weight pairs, and practice questions love to mix them. A child under eight and under eighty pounds needs a weight-appropriate restraint, while the rear-seat rule near an active front air bag covers a child under five and under forty pounds. So eight goes with eighty, and five goes with forty. A distractor might pair eight with forty, or five with eighty, and it will look almost right. Match the numbers carefully, then ask which question is being asked: what restraint the child uses, or where the child must sit.

lines.text: Under eight, forty to eighty pounds.
Only if no seat has a lap and shoulder belt.
A properly fitted lap belt alone.

narration.text: There is one narrow exception to the restraint rule. If no seat has a lap and shoulder belt for the restraint, a child under eight weighing forty to eighty pounds may ride with a properly fitted lap belt alone. This exists for older vehicles that have only lap belts in some or all seats, where a booster cannot be used correctly. The condition is strict. If any seat has a lap and shoulder belt for the restraint, the exception does not apply, and the child uses the weight-appropriate restraint in that seat. A short trip or a convenient seat does not unlock the exception.

lines.text: Lap belt low on the hips.
Shoulder belt across shoulder and chest.

narration.text: Children who have outgrown safety seats should use federally compliant booster seats until an adult belt fits properly. Good fit means the lap belt is snug on the hips, not the stomach, and the shoulder belt crosses the shoulder and chest, not the face or throat. A booster raises the child so the adult belt lands in those safe places. Moving to the adult belt too early can cause serious injuries, because a belt across the stomach or neck can harm the soft parts of the body in a crash. Belt fit, not a birthday, is the real test.

Here is a quick check: a parent is driving a four-year-old who weighs thirty-five pounds. The car has an active front passenger air bag and a rear seat, and the child's restraint is not built for use with a front air bag. Where must the child sit? Work it out before reading on. The answer is the rear seat. When a vehicle has an active front passenger air bag and a rear seat, a child under five weighing under forty pounds must ride in the rear unless the restraint is built for use with a front air bag. The child also needs a weight-appropriate restraint.

lines.text: Eight and eighty; five and forty.

narration.text: Let us recap. Correctly used safety seats could save seven of every ten children who die unrestrained, and the best seat is one used every ride that fits your car, with low-cost rentals often available. A driver must restrain every passenger under sixteen. A child under eight and under eighty pounds needs a weight-appropriate restraint, and a child under five and under forty pounds rides in back near an active front air bag. A lap belt alone is allowed for a child under eight at forty to eighty pounds only if no seat has a lap and shoulder belt. Use a booster until the adult belt fits.

why_how.text: Air bags deploy with great force, so seating and belt position decide whether they protect or injure.
Riders and children in open spaces lack a vehicle's protection, so helmets and pickup bed limits fill the gap.

result.text: The fourteen-year-old rides buckled in the cab instead.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a DOT sticker added to any helmet makes it legal.

correction.text: Only a DOT symbol fixed permanently by the manufacturer marks a compliant helmet; a sticker sold separately or added later does not.

prompt.text: A fourteen-year-old wants to ride in the open bed of the family pickup to the lake. Is that allowed, and who is responsible?

answer.text: No. Children under sixteen may not ride in an open pickup bed, and the driver is responsible.

rationale.text: The pickup bed law uses age sixteen, unlike the rear-seat advice for children twelve and under.

lines.text: Helmets and pickup beds have rules.

narration.text: This final lesson in the chapter gathers several protection rules. You will learn how forcefully air bags deploy and what that means for children, where children should ride, how to position belts and seats around air bags, the motorcycle and moped helmet law and how to recognize a compliant helmet, and the law against children riding in open pickup beds. Some of these are firm laws, and some are strong advice. Practice questions test the difference, especially between the rear-seat advice for young children and the pickup bed law for older children.

title.text: The force of an air bag

lines.text: Up to two hundred miles per hour.

narration.text: An air bag bursts out of the dashboard at up to two hundred miles per hour, faster than an eye blink, so it is far from a soft pillow. That force is what lets it protect an adult in a crash, but it can seriously injure someone who is too close or too small. Because of that, the handbook advises that children aged twelve and younger ride buckled up in a rear seat. And an infant in a rear-facing safety seat must never ride in the front seat of a vehicle that has a passenger-side air bag, because the bag would strike the back of the seat right behind the baby's head.

lines.text: Lap belt under the abdomen, low on hips.
Shoulder belt across collarbone and breastbone.
Seats as far back as practical.

narration.text: Air bags only supplement belts, so the belts must be positioned correctly. Wear the lap belt under the abdomen and low on the hips. Wear the shoulder belt over the collarbone, away from the neck and across the breastbone. These are the strong parts of the body that can take the load of a crash. Distance matters too. Move the driver and front passenger seats as far back as practical, especially for shorter people, so there is room for the air bag to inflate before it reaches you. Close seating and a loose belt are the combinations that turn an air bag into a hazard.

lines.text: Rear seat: advised for twelve and under.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Two child rules use different ages, and one is advice while the other is law. Riding in the rear seat is advised for children twelve and under, while riding in an open pickup bed is prohibited by law for children under sixteen. North Carolina bars children younger than sixteen from riding in the open bed of a pickup truck, and the driver is responsible for compliance, though the statute has some exemptions. So a fourteen-year-old may ride in the front seat under the advice, but may not ride in a pickup bed under the law. Keep twelve with advice and sixteen with law.

lines.text: Federal Safety Standard two hundred eighteen.

narration.text: Every motorcycle or moped operator and passenger must wear a safety helmet meeting Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard two hundred eighteen. That covers both people on the bike, and it covers mopeds as well as motorcycles. A compliant helmet has a firm polystyrene liner about one inch thick, and a DOT symbol fixed permanently on the back by the maker. Novelty helmets that look similar but lack the thick, firm liner do not meet the standard. The liner is what absorbs the force of an impact, so it is the part that truly protects a rider's head in a crash.

Here is a second trap. Some riders buy DOT stickers and attach them to novelty helmets, hoping to look legal. A DOT symbol fixed permanently by the manufacturer marks a compliant helmet, while a DOT sticker sold separately or added by the rider does not. The handbook is clear that a sticker added later does not make a helmet legal. So the question is never whether the letters appear on the helmet, but who put them there and whether the helmet underneath meets the standard. The memory line: sticker is not compliance. Look for the maker's symbol and the firm liner.

lines.text: Open pickup bed to the lake.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a family is driving to the lake, and their fourteen-year-old asks to ride in the open bed of the pickup with the coolers. Is that allowed, and who is responsible? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no, and the driver is responsible. North Carolina bars children younger than sixteen from riding in the open bed of a pickup truck, with some exemptions in the statute. The pickup bed law uses age sixteen, unlike the rear-seat advice for children twelve and under. The teen should ride buckled up in the cab.

lines.text: Air bags hit hard; seats back.
Maker's DOT helmet; no kids in pickup beds.

narration.text: To finish the chapter, an air bag deploys at up to two hundred miles per hour, so children twelve and younger should ride buckled in back, and a rear-facing infant never rides in front of a passenger air bag. Wear the lap belt low on the hips and the shoulder belt across the collarbone and breastbone, and move front seats as far back as practical. Every motorcycle or moped operator and passenger wears a helmet meeting the federal standard, marked by the maker's permanent DOT symbol, not a sticker. And children under sixteen may not ride in an open pickup bed.
